title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: Tertia — violatio conditionis ≠ poena
pass_a_gloss: Third, violation of the condition or precept is not a penalty denounced to the transgressor. But privation of justice is violation of the condition or precept. Therefore it is not a penalty denounced to the transgressor. The major needs no proof: the minor I demonstrate thus. What the law forbids is a violation of the law. But the law forbids absence of justice in a man (as certainly as it commands justice to be in a man). Therefore absence of justice (which for you is spiritual death) is a violation of the law.
pass_b_english: Third proof: breaking the condition or precept is not itself the penalty announced against the breaker. But loss of righteousness is breaking the condition or precept. Therefore that loss is not the announced penalty. The major is obvious; I prove the minor as follows. Whatever the law forbids is a breach of the law. The law forbids righteousness being absent from a man as firmly as it commands righteousness to be in him. Therefore that absence—which you call spiritual death—is a breach of the law.
source_text: Tertia, violatio conditionis sive praecepti non est poena transgressori denunciata. Sed privatio justitiae est violatio conditionis seu praecepti. Ergo non est poena transgressori denunciata. Major probatione non eget: Minorem sic demonstro. Quod lex prohibet, id legis violatio est. At lex prohibet absentiam justitiae in homine (tam certe quam jubet homini justitiam inesse.) Ergo absentia justitiae (quae tibi mors est spiritualis) violatio est legis.

choices.why: Opens Tertia; minor via law forbidding absence

notes: Cap. IV Secunda ratio densify section 227 from locked 1661 Latin (pp. 195 tip–198 tip).
